Hemocytes, the immune cells of invertebrates, are essential for defending against pathogens and repairing wounds. In *Drosophila melanogaster* embryos, these cells originate from a specific region called the ventral furrow and migrate outward to colonize the entire embryo. This study investigates the collective movement of these cells by analyzing their behavior in both two and three dimensions. We observed that the cells exhibit a unique migration pattern characterized by a "tango," where they move in a coordinated, circular fashion around a central point. This behavior is driven by a combination of local interactions and global cues. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the cells' movement is influenced by the geometry of the space they occupy, with the cells tending to align along the boundaries of the available area. These findings provide new insights into the mechanisms governing hemocyte migration and may have broader implications for understanding the collective movement of other cell types.

This study introduces a contrastive Siamese network designed for semi-supervised speech recognition. The proposed architecture employs a Siamese framework to extract shared features from paired audio segments, while integrating contrastive learning to align these features with their corresponding text labels. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves a 20% reduction in Word Error Rate (WER) on the LibriSpeech test-clean dataset when utilizing only 10% of the training data.

This document details the most recent version of the axial and vector inelastic structure functions for lepton-nucleon scattering, which are derived from the nucleon's spin-flip and non-spin-flip generalized parton distributions (GPDs). The analysis incorporates the Regge behavior of Regge trajectories for nucleon resonances, alongside Regge exchanges for baryon and meson exchanges. The axial structure function is further refined by including contributions from the pion and eta mesons. The study also examines the impact of varying nucleon and resonance Regge trajectories, as well as the meson Regge exchanges, on these structure functions.

This paper addresses the challenge of designing an adaptive control law for linear-quadratic (LQ) systems featuring a hidden Markov chain, with the objective of ensuring almost sure stabilization. The proposed solution utilizes a combination of a certainty equivalence approach and a Riccati equation framework. The study demonstrates that the resulting control law achieves almost sure stabilization under specific conditions. Furthermore, it establishes that the closed-loop system's state remains exponentially mean-square stable provided the system is stochastically stabilizable.

This study introduces a multi-modal and multi-factor branching time active inference framework designed to model the brain's capacity for integrating diverse sensory inputs. The model employs a hierarchical architecture where lower levels encode specific sensory modalities, while higher levels synthesize these inputs into a unified representation. The proposed approach is evaluated through a simulated scenario involving a robot navigating a maze, tasked with locating a goal while avoiding obstacles. The results demonstrate that the model effectively integrates information from various sensory sources to achieve its objectives.

We examine the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation within the context of a cold quark gluon plasma, specifically analyzing the dynamics of the energy-momentum tensor component $T_{00}$ in the hydrodynamic limit. Our findings indicate that the resulting KdV soliton solutions are characterized by the speed of sound and the plasma's temperature.
We establish that a k-space is Eberlein-Grothendieck precisely when it can be embedded as a closed subset within a product of Banach spaces endowed with the weak topology.
We establish a comprehensive classification of smooth planar vector fields featuring a center that exhibit isochronicity within a neighborhood of said center.

This study introduces a novel approach to analyze the formation of periodic orbits within the Lorenz system. By utilizing a similarity metric, we generate similarity signature curves that reveal the existence of these orbits. Our findings indicate that the Lorenz system's signature curves exhibit a distinctive pattern resembling a "W," which serves as a reliable indicator for periodic orbit formation.

This paper examines the local asymptotic normality (LAN) property for the solution distributions of stochastic differential equations driven by Levy processes. We establish that the LAN property holds for these solution families under specific regularity conditions, which are detailed herein.

We demonstrate that the Teichmüller group Γ acts on the space of square-integrable functions on a Riemann surface Σ via a unitary representation. This representation is constructed using the twisted Laplacian, which is defined by a closed 1-form on Σ whose cohomology class is invariant under the action of Γ. We establish that the resulting spectrum is discrete and consists of infinitely many eigenvalues, each possessing a finite multiplicity. Furthermore, we prove that the corresponding eigenfunctions are automorphic with respect to Γ. Finally, we show that the associated eigenvalues are bounded from below by a constant that depends only on the genus of Σ.

We introduce FNetAR, a novel architecture that combines the strengths of autoregressive transformers and Fourier-based transformers. This approach utilizes a Fourier transform to convert input sequences into the frequency domain, where a lightweight autoregressive transformer generates predictions for the missing components. The model then applies an inverse Fourier transform to reconstruct the original sequence. This design offers a highly efficient solution for sequence modeling, requiring only a minimal autoregressive transformer with a small number of parameters. Empirical results demonstrate that FNetAR achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art autoregressive transformers while utilizing significantly fewer parameters.

This study examines the evolution of the universe within the framework of Saez-Ballester's scalar-tensor theory, specifically analyzing a generalized ghost pilgrim dark energy model. We derive the corresponding cosmological field equations and investigate the model's behavior across both matter-dominated and dark energy-dominated eras. Furthermore, we analyze the model's dynamics using a phase space approach.

This study examines the optimization of Service Function Chaining (SFC) within Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) environments. In MEC, the SFC process involves selecting an optimal sequence of Virtual Network Functions (VNFs) to satisfy specific Quality of Service (QoS) requirements. We model this selection as a non-cooperative game where each VNF acts as a rational agent aiming to maximize its own utility. We demonstrate that the game possesses a unique Nash Equilibrium (NE) and propose a Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithm to efficiently identify this equilibrium. Furthermore, we evaluate the proposed RL method against traditional heuristic approaches, showing that it achieves superior performance in terms of both convergence speed and the quality of the resulting equilibria.

We examine a random Dirac fermion model featuring a stochastic mass term, where the mass magnitude is fixed but its phase varies randomly. This randomness breaks chiral symmetry, resulting in a finite correlation length. By applying the functional renormalization group, we identify a non-Gaussian fixed point that governs the system's infrared behavior. Our analysis reveals that the system exhibits a first-order phase transition, characterized by a discontinuity in the order parameter.

Although depression is a prevalent mental health condition, research has predominantly focused on its negative symptoms, leaving a gap in understanding the positive experiences of those suffering from it. This study addresses that gap by analyzing the positive moments of 1,000 individuals diagnosed with depression, utilizing a dataset of 1,000 Reddit comments tagged with depression and happiness. We developed a novel approach to identify these positive instances by employing a BERT-based model to detect sentiment polarity. Our analysis reveals that the positive moments of depressed individuals are characterized by a strong emphasis on social interactions, particularly with family and friends.

We investigate the impact of isospin breaking in the context of Sp(4) gauge theory with two flavors, utilizing a framework of two degenerate quarks with opposite electric charges. This setup is realized through the addition of a mass term to the Lagrangian, which breaks isospin symmetry. Our analysis employs lattice simulations conducted at a single lattice spacing, specifically targeting the regime of strong coupling.

We report the synthesis and characterization of a novel tellurate compound, Na$_{4-\delta}$NiTeO$_{6}$, which features zigzag magnetic chains of $S$ = 1 Ni$^{2+}$ ions. This material exhibits a magnetic ordering temperature of $T_{\rm N} = 10.5$ K, accompanied by a distinct anomaly in the specific heat. Analysis of the magnetic susceptibility and heat capacity data using the Ising model for zigzag chains yields an exchange coupling constant of $J = 1.2$ meV. Furthermore, the compound displays a magnetization plateau at $1/3$ of the saturation value under a magnetic field applied parallel to the zigzag direction.

Smart vehicular networks (SVNs) are anticipated to transform the transportation sector by enabling autonomous vehicles to communicate with one another and with infrastructure. However, the inherent uncertainty in these networks, stemming from unpredictable human behavior and the dynamic nature of the environment, creates significant challenges for trust management. This paper introduces a conceptual framework for trust management within SVNs, designed to address these uncertainties. The proposed approach integrates a Bayesian inference model with a fuzzy logic system to evaluate trustworthiness. The fuzzy logic component is specifically employed to handle uncertainty in the data collected from vehicles and infrastructure. Furthermore, the framework incorporates a trust propagation mechanism to facilitate the sharing of trustworthiness information across the network.

This paper introduces a monotone cubic spline interpolation method designed for functions exhibiting strong monotonicity. The approach is validated through numerical experiments using various functions, including those that are merely monotonic, alongside tests on the Rosenbrock function.

We present a new class of exact black bounces featuring scalar hair within AdS-Taub-NUT spacetimes. These solutions are derived by applying a specific analytic continuation to the AdS-Taub-NUT metric, which is known to admit scalar hair. The resulting geometry is characterized by a complex scalar field configuration and a metric that is complex-valued.

Sound ontologies, such as the widely used Extended Sound Event Ontology (ESOX), are essential for organizing audio data and supporting research in fields like audio forensics and speech enhancement. However, their extensive size and complexity make manual annotation of new sound classes a significant challenge. This paper introduces a novel annotation framework designed to streamline the creation of new sound classes within large ontologies. By leveraging existing ontological structures, the system automatically generates initial labels and descriptions for new entries, thereby reducing the manual workload. We evaluated this approach using the ESOX taxonomy and conducted a user study with 12 participants. The results indicate that our method substantially lowers the effort required for annotation while maintaining high-quality outcomes.

This review examines the application of dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) to complex systems, with a specific focus on its utility in modeling ecosystems and chemical reaction networks. The text begins by outlining the fundamental principles of DMFT and the methodology for deriving self-consistent equations. It subsequently explores the theory's application to the Lotka-Volterra model, demonstrating how DMFT can yield exact solutions for the system's dynamics. The discussion then shifts to chemical reaction networks, where the authors demonstrate that DMFT can generate exact equations for the time evolution of mean concentrations. Finally, the review concludes by addressing the limitations of the mean-field approach and proposing potential extensions to enhance its applicability.

We examine the characteristics of avalanches within a classical spin model defined on a Cayley tree. Our findings indicate that the probability distribution for avalanche sizes, $P(S)$, follows a power law, $P(S) \sim S^{-\tau}$, where the exponent $\tau$ is determined by the system's parameters.

This paper introduces a novel framework for representing discourse connections through question answering. We propose that discourse connections can be effectively represented as questions that link sentences, where the answers to these questions are derived from the text itself. We outline a three-stage pipeline for this approach: first, generating questions that connect sentences; second, retrieving the specific answers from the text; and third, encoding these question-answer pairs to form the final representation. We evaluate this framework using a dataset of 1,000 passages from the RST corpus, where each passage consists of multiple sentences and associated connection types. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves performance comparable to current state-of-the-art discourse comprehension systems.

This review examines Perfectly Matched Layers (PMLs) applied to hyperbolic wave propagation equations, with a specific focus on the PML implementation for the Helmholtz equation. We explore the theoretical foundations of PMLs, their numerical discretization, and the associated error analysis. Furthermore, the text addresses the challenges of PMLs when used with high-order discretization schemes and concludes by discussing the PML's application in modeling wave propagation within inhomogeneous media.

This study investigates the deformation and fragmentation of droplets within a liquid array under laser irradiation. The laser's energy absorption by the droplets triggers a rapid temperature rise, leading to vaporization and the formation of a vapor bubble. The resulting pressure from this bubble drives the deformation and subsequent fragmentation of the droplets. The research examines how laser pulse duration, energy, and the droplet's initial state influence these outcomes. The findings demonstrate that the laser pulse duration and energy are critical factors in determining the deformation and fragmentation of the droplets.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly expanding, with billions of devices expected to connect to the Internet by 2025. This surge in connectivity is expected to generate massive volumes of data, creating significant challenges for network infrastructure. To address these issues, this paper introduces a framework that integrates Software-Defined Networking (SDN) and Publish/Subscribe (Pub/Sub) mechanisms to orchestrate IoT traffic. The proposed solution utilizes an SDN-based control plane to manage network resources and a Pub/Sub-based data plane to facilitate efficient data dissemination. The study evaluates the framework's performance through simulations, demonstrating its ability to handle IoT traffic effectively.

We establish the corresponding vector-valued gyrotriangle inequality and prove that the proposed distance fulfills the requirements of a gyrometric functional. Furthermore, we define a specific linear combination of these distances, which serves as a valid metric for the SPD space.

This study examines the detection of travel time anisotropy in the subsurface using horizontal magnetic field data. We demonstrate that the horizontal component of the magnetic field is sensitive to the vertical component of the group velocity, which is itself influenced by the P-wave velocity structure and the S-to-P velocity ratio. Consequently, the horizontal magnetic field can reveal travel time anisotropy, provided that the S-to-P velocity ratio is known.

We introduce a topologically protected, on-chip squeezed light generator. This system utilizes a photonic chip featuring a topological edge state to circulate light, which is then squeezed via a nonlinear process. The design is robust against fabrication imperfections and scattering losses, and it can be implemented using existing silicon photonics technology.

This study introduces a method for generating smooth, time-optimal trajectories for quadcopters, a critical component for executing agile maneuvers. The approach employs a two-stage optimization strategy: first, a preliminary trajectory is created using a time-weighted sum of splines, and subsequently, a second optimization phase refines this path to achieve time-optimality while maintaining smoothness. The paper details the mathematical formulation of this two-step process and provides numerical results demonstrating the method's efficacy.

This paper investigates the algebraic structure of $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-linear conjucyclic codes within $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}[x]/\langle x^n+1\rangle$, where $n$ is a positive integer coprime to $q$. We establish a one-to-one correspondence between these codes and a specific subset of $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}[x]/\langle x^n+1\rangle$, denoted as $\mathcal{C}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that $\mathcal{C}$ forms a commutative subring within the quotient ring $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}[x]/\langle x^n+1\rangle$. Additionally, we define a mapping $\Phi$ that establishes a bijection between $\mathcal{C}$ and the set of $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-linear circulant codes in the same quotient ring. We prove that $\Phi$ is an isomorphism, thereby confirming that $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-linear conjucyclic codes possess an algebraic structure isomorphic to that of $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-linear circulant codes.

This topical group examined the community's engagement with the broader society, specifically focusing on the roles of the community and its members. It began by outlining the community's current state and its future aspirations, then identified the specific skills and competences necessary to achieve these goals. The group also analyzed the current landscape of community engagement, pinpointing both the strengths and limitations of the existing model. Finally, it proposed a new framework for community engagement, detailing the essential elements required for its successful implementation.

This study presents the first measurement of the $W$ boson polarisation in top-antitop ($t\bar{t}$) events, utilizing 20.3 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data at $\sqrt{s}$ = 8 TeV recorded by the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The analysis focuses on the lepton+jets decay channel, where the polarisation is derived from the angular distribution of charged leptons originating from $W$ boson decays. The resulting fraction of longitudinally polarised $W$ bosons is determined to be $0.682 \pm 0.014$ (stat) $\pm 0.014$ (syst), with the statistical and systematic uncertainties respectively. This result aligns with the Standard Model prediction of $0.695 \pm 0.014$ (syst).

The power hypergraph of a graph $G$, denoted $G^k$, is a hypergraph where every edge consists of $k+1$ vertices, formed by taking all $(k+1)$-cliques of $G$. The power hypergraph's eigenvalues are defined as the roots of its characteristic polynomial. This paper establishes that the eigenvalues of $G^k$ are identical to the eigenvalues of a specific signed graph derived from $G$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the spectrum of $G^k$ is uniquely determined by $G$.

This study examines the performance of localizing individual satellites within the Starlink constellation, which relies on inter-satellite links (ISLs) to form a cooperative network. By utilizing measurements from these ISLs, the system can determine the relative positions of satellites. We analyze the accuracy of this localization by establishing performance bounds based on the Cramér-Rao lower bound (CRLB) and the Bernstein lower bound. Our findings indicate that the CRLB is highly sensitive to the specific measurement model employed, whereas the Bernstein lower bound remains largely unaffected by such modeling variations.

We report the discovery of transit timing variations (TTVs) in the hot Jupiter XO-3b, which are attributed to gravitational interactions with an unseen companion. By analyzing 12 transit events spanning 10 years, we identified a TTV amplitude of 10.5 ± 1.5 minutes. This signal aligns with a companion having a mass of 0.01–0.02 M_Jup and an orbital period of 10–20 days. The observed TTVs are consistent with a companion located near a 2:1 mean motion resonance, a configuration that would naturally result in high eccentricity. Furthermore, the TTVs are consistent with tidal evolution models that predict the system's eccentricity will decay over time.

The 21-cm signal from neutral hydrogen is a highly sought-after target for cosmological research, yet it is extremely faint and obscured by terrestrial radio interference. To address this, the signal is measured against a noise wave, which is subsequently subtracted from the data. This process is complicated by the fact that the noise wave's characteristics fluctuate over time. This paper introduces a Bayesian framework for calibrating the noise wave, which is designed to be computationally efficient and adaptable to various experimental setups. We demonstrate the method's efficacy using simulated data from the CHIME/FRB telescope, which is also employed as a global 21-cm experiment.

This paper establishes a formula for the genus $g$ Gromov-Witten invariants associated with a projective bundle over a smooth base variety. The formula expresses these invariants as integrals involving certain $\psi$-classes and pullbacks of the base variety's invariants. This result extends a formula previously derived by Pandharipande and Schmitt for the case where $g=0$.
This paper establishes highly uniform versions of the prime number theorem, which are applicable to numerous arithmetical functions.

This study introduces a novel methodology for analyzing Alzheimer's disease clinical trials, utilizing natural cubic splines to model the underlying trajectory of cognitive decline. By fitting these splines to longitudinal data, the approach estimates the rate of decline for each participant. These individual estimates are subsequently used to evaluate treatment efficacy, with the method's performance validated through simulations and an application to data from the Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study.

This paper introduces a parking guidance system designed for smart cities, leveraging a crowdsourcing approach to monitor parking availability. The system utilizes a fleet of autonomous vehicles to gather parking data, which is then transmitted to a central server for processing. The server subsequently distributes parking recommendations to mobile applications on users' devices. The study details the system's architecture, outlines the algorithm for generating parking suggestions, and evaluates its performance through simulations.

Flat minima optimization strategies, such as sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) and stochastic weight averaging (SWA), are designed to locate flat regions within the loss landscape. This study investigates the efficacy of these methods in the context of overparameterized neural networks. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, these algorithms fail to identify flat minima. Furthermore, we introduce a novel approach termed "flatness-aware initialization" (FAI), which successfully locates flat minima even when SAM and SWA are ineffective.

This paper introduces a new reflective parametric frequency selective limiter (FPFSL) designed to achieve sub-dB insertion loss and a power threshold in the microwatt range. The device utilizes a microstrip line resonator to select specific frequencies and a Josephson junction-based parametric limiter to suppress signals exceeding a defined threshold. The system operates by applying a pump tone to the parametric limiter, which modulates its impedance; this modulation is then reflected back through the microstrip line resonator. The resulting reflection coefficient varies with the input signal's amplitude, enabling the device to attenuate high-power signals while passing low-power signals with minimal loss. The authors present a theoretical model for the parametric limiter and validate it through experimental results. The measured insertion loss for low-power signals is 0.1 dB, while the measured power threshold is 1.5 mW.

This study introduces a novel SEIRS model designed to analyze the COVID-19 pandemic under the specific assumption that no lasting immunity exists. In this framework, the transition from the recovered compartment back to the susceptible one occurs at a rate equal to the natural birth rate, effectively treating the entire population as susceptible over time. The authors derive the basic reproduction number, $R_0$, and establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for disease extinction. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that the model admits a unique globally asymptotically stable disease-free equilibrium whenever $R_0 < 1$.

We present a straightforward yet effective method for selecting context in word embeddings. This approach is designed to be compatible with any word embedding model and requires no additional training. Our experiments demonstrate that this selection technique enhances the performance of various downstream applications, including word similarity assessments, analogy resolution, and part-of-speech tagging.

This study examines the distribution of $k$-clusters within high-intensity random geometric graphs. We derive a precise asymptotic formula for the expected count of these $k$-clusters, demonstrating that the relative variance of the cluster count diminishes as the graph intensity approaches infinity. Furthermore, we establish a concentration inequality for the cluster count that remains valid across a broad spectrum of distributions, including those with heavy tails.

We introduce a new approach for building rotating stars, which relies on a Lagrangian framework to model the fluid's motion. This method is advantageous because it avoids the complexities associated with the Eulerian formalism, particularly the need to solve partial differential equations. Instead, our technique utilizes a set of ordinary differential equations to determine the trajectories of individual fluid particles. We demonstrate that this approach can generate rotating stars with arbitrary shapes, provided the necessary boundary conditions are met.

This study examines the Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi (LTB) spacetime within the Palatini formulation of $f(R)$ gravity, where the Ricci scalar $R$ is a function of the metric tensor $g_{\mu\nu}$. We demonstrate that the modified Einstein equations yield an additional constraint on the LTB metric, which is absent in standard General Relativity. This extra constraint is expressed as a function of the Ricci scalar $R$ and the energy density $\rho$. Furthermore, we analyze the spacetime's singularity structure and its implications for the Big Bang singularity.

We demonstrate that any $N$-partite system can be rendered completely nonlocal via local operations and classical communication (LOCC) utilizing a set of product states. This finding establishes that strong quantum nonlocality is universal across all $N$-partite systems under the one-way LOCC framework.

This study introduces a novel approach to predicting visual attention on web pages by leveraging gaze data analytics. The method utilizes a sliding window technique to forecast attention continuously, with the window size determined by the specific task. The study evaluates the proposed method's effectiveness through a comprehensive analysis of its performance across various tasks and window sizes.

Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) are poised to become a cornerstone of sixth-generation (6G) wireless networks, offering a cost-effective method to enhance spectral efficiency and coverage. While current RIS implementations rely on reflective elements, this study introduces a novel transmissive RIS architecture designed to boost the capacity of multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MU-MIMO) systems. The research details the design and fabrication of a 28 GHz transmissive RIS prototype, which was experimentally validated in a 28 GHz MU-MIMO scenario. The findings demonstrate that this transmissive RIS significantly elevates MU-MIMO capacity, outperforming both standard RIS and conventional MU-MIMO systems.

Offline reinforcement learning (RL) seeks to optimize policies using only historical data, without further interaction with the environment. While recent research has largely focused on linear function approximation, this paper extends the linear-programming framework to accommodate general function approximators. We introduce a novel algorithm that leverages the dual relationship between primal and dual problems to derive a tight upper bound on the suboptimality gap. This approach yields a sample complexity of $\tilde{O}(dH^2/\epsilon)$, where $d$ represents the dimensionality of the function approximator, $H$ is the episode length, and $\epsilon$ denotes the error tolerance. This complexity matches the best-known results for linear function approximation and is optimal up to logarithmic factors. Furthermore, our method offers a more straightforward proof compared to prior approaches and provides a tighter bound on the suboptimality gap.

We present a method for constructing a free, cofibrantly generated, and proper model category of simplicial sets equipped with a given set of homotopies, provided the homotopies satisfy certain conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this homotopy theory is equivalent to the homotopy theory of the associated $\infty$-groupoid.

Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) is a technique that maps the spatial distribution of fluorescence lifetimes, a property that remains independent of fluorophore concentration. This technique is widely utilized in biological research to investigate cellular structures and functions. However, the spatial resolution of FLIM is constrained by the diffraction limit of light. To address this, we introduce a deconvolution method designed to enhance the spatial resolution of FLIM images. This approach employs a non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) algorithm to separate the observed image into a high-resolution component and a point spread function (PSF). By applying a deconvolution process to the high-resolution component, we successfully recover a high-resolution FLIM image.

Personalized product search aims to deliver tailored results to users by leveraging their individual behavior. While existing methods typically rely on user-item interaction data to construct user profiles, they often overlook the influence of other users' behaviors. This study introduces a new framework that integrates both user-item interactions and user-user relationships to enhance personalized product search. Specifically, we model user-user connections as a graph and employ Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) to capture the impact of peer behaviors. Furthermore, we incorporate a multi-head attention mechanism to weigh the significance of different users within the graph. Experimental results on two real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

Graph representation learning has garnered significant attention in recent years, particularly for its applications in recommendation systems and natural language processing. However, existing methods often fail to adequately capture the intrinsic manifold structures inherent in graph data. To address this, we introduce a novel unsupervised framework for graph representation learning that simultaneously models both the manifold structure and node attributes. Our approach employs a deep neural network to learn a nonlinear mapping from the original graph space to a latent representation space, thereby preserving the manifold structure. Furthermore, we integrate node attribute information into the manifold structure to enhance the representation quality. To achieve this, we propose a new objective function that jointly optimizes the manifold structure and node attributes. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches.

This study introduces a two-stage genetic algorithm designed to create non-orthogonal sequences for grant-free massive connectivity scenarios. The first stage employs a genetic algorithm to generate an initial population of sequences, while the second stage utilizes another genetic algorithm to evolve these sequences into the final output. The proposed method is evaluated against existing techniques, including orthogonal sequences, random sequences, and those derived from the Kasami set. The results demonstrate that the suggested approach yields sequences with lower cross-correlation values and a more uniform distribution of cross-correlation levels compared to the benchmark methods.

This study introduces an innovative approach to blind compressed sensing (CS) that leverages the known structure of the sensing matrix. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the original signal can be recovered from its compressed measurements by solving a combinatorial optimization problem. This method is particularly effective for signals with a sparse representation in a known basis, such as images, where the sensing matrix is constructed from the dictionary of a known sparsifying basis. By exploiting this structural knowledge, the proposed technique achieves superior performance compared to traditional CS methods, which typically rely on random sensing matrices.

This study introduces a novel method for domain adaptation that employs adversarial training to align the source and target domains. The approach utilizes a discriminator to minimize the discrepancy between the transformed source domain and the target domain, while simultaneously training a generator to produce transformations that successfully match these distributions. The generator is optimized to minimize the discriminator's loss, whereas the discriminator is trained to maximize it. The proposed framework is evaluated on CIFAR-10 and SVHN datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This paper investigates local derivations defined on Jordan matrix rings over commutative involutive rings. We demonstrate that every local derivation on these structures corresponds to a standard derivation. Furthermore, we establish that all local derivations on Jordan matrix rings are identically zero.

This study examines the gravitational lensing of a Dirac monopole within the framework of Berry's phase. We demonstrate that Berry's phase undergoes a shift proportional to the solid angle subtended by the image of the monopole, as observed from the source. Furthermore, we establish that this shift is quantized in units of $2\pi$ times the monopole's magnetic charge.

This study investigates the impact of spin-orbit coupling on compacton solutions within two-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensates. We demonstrate that compacton solutions persist in the presence of spin-orbit coupling, provided the coupling strength remains below a critical threshold. Furthermore, we analyze the spin-orbit coupling's influence on the spin density profile, revealing that the spin density exhibits a periodic structure.

We examine the $\Lambda_c(2595)^+$ and $\Lambda_c(2625)^+$ states within the framework of the heavy quark spin symmetry (HQSS) and the diquark model. Our analysis indicates that the $\Lambda_c(2595)^+$ is likely a $1/2^-$ state, whereas the $\Lambda_c(2625)^+$ is probably a $3/2^-$ state. Consequently, these two states do not constitute a heavy quark spin symmetry partner pair.

This paper demonstrates that any continuous function defined on the orbit space of a compact Lie group $G$ acting smoothly on a compact manifold $M$ can be approximated by functions that are continuous on the orbit space and are constructed from smooth functions on $M$ that are invariant under the action of $G$.

This white paper outlines the potential of high-energy muon colliders to probe axion-like particles (ALPs) and the strong dynamics responsible for generating their masses. We examine the production and decay mechanisms of ALPs at these facilities, along with the associated experimental challenges. Furthermore, we analyze the implications of recent LHC findings on the gluon-gluon fusion process for ALP production, alongside the theoretical framework of the QCD axion. Finally, we explore the potential for muon colliders to investigate the strong force sector, specifically focusing on the potential existence of light pions.

This paper introduces MetaSys, a practical open-source framework designed to facilitate the implementation and assessment of cross-layer optimizations. MetaSys enables the creation of metadata management systems that can be integrated into various open-source networking stacks, including Linux, Mininet, and NS-3. It provides a comprehensive suite of tools for defining, executing, and evaluating these optimizations. The authors demonstrate the framework's utility by implementing and testing two specific cross-layer optimizations: (1) a cross-layer approach to flowlet switching and (2) a cross-layer method for managing flowlet size.

This study introduces a new transfer learning framework for image classification that leverages synthetic data. The approach employs a Siamese network to learn a metric space where the distance between images corresponds to their semantic similarity. By utilizing synthetic data, the model learns to map images into this space, enabling the subsequent classification of real-world data through the identification of the nearest neighbors within the synthetic set. The paper details the methodology, presents experimental findings, and discusses the associated challenges.

This paper examines a singular quasilinear elliptic system featuring convection terms and unbounded coefficients, subject to Dirichlet conditions on bounded domains with smooth boundaries. The analysis employs a fixed point approach to establish the existence of a positive solution.

This paper introduces a novel recurrent unit designed to capture long-term dependencies through the lens of Fourier analysis. We demonstrate that the Fourier transform of a sequence generated by our unit adheres to a closed-form expression, enabling the model to learn extended dependencies with a constant number of parameters. Furthermore, we prove that the unit's architecture is capable of universal approximation. Empirical evaluations on the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) benchmark tasks confirm that our unit surpasses standard recurrent units in terms of performance.

This study examines the challenge of identifying the optimal policy within a Markov Decision Process (MDP) under the assumption that the environment's dynamics are known. We introduce a novel algorithm, named MDP-UCB, which is designed to locate this optimal policy. The method operates by utilizing a specific set of state-action pairs to estimate the value of each policy, with the goal of determining the best one. We establish a theoretical upper bound on the regret associated with MDP-UCB, demonstrating that it scales logarithmically with the time horizon. Furthermore, we prove that this bound is tight by deriving a matching lower bound. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our approach through numerical experiments.

We introduce a novel dual-wake injection technique for producing highly brilliant, linearly polarized attosecond electron bunches. This approach utilizes two laser-driven plasma wakes, each generated by a separate laser pulse, to sequentially capture and accelerate electrons. The first wake, driven by a longer pulse, injects electrons into the second wake, which is driven by a shorter pulse. This second stage is optimized to generate a single, high-quality electron bunch. The method's efficacy is validated through particle-in-cell simulations, which demonstrate that the resulting attosecond electron bunch possesses a high degree of linear polarization.

This paper explores the evolution of complexity in living systems, focusing on the emergence of new traits and the adaptation of existing ones. It examines how the interplay between natural selection and random mutations drives the development of complexity in organisms, while also considering the roles of environmental factors and internal constraints. The authors argue that the evolution of complexity is a universal phenomenon that can be observed across different scales, from the molecular to the ecosystem level. They suggest that the evolution of complexity is a fundamental aspect of life that can be understood through the lens of thermodynamics and information theory. This study examines the utility of open-source repositories and artificial intelligence in mapping climate change research to inform R&D policy. We evaluated the performance of various AI-driven tools, including text mining, topic modeling, and network analysis, in extracting insights from open-source data. Our findings indicate that while these methods offer significant advantages for evidence-based policy making, they also present limitations that must be addressed.

This paper introduces ASVAAN, a semi-automatic framework designed to facilitate side-channel analysis of Android Native Development Kit (NDK) applications. ASVAAN streamlines the creation of test applications and the execution of analysis by automatically generating necessary code and managing the test environment. It supports both power and electromagnetic (EM) analyses, offering a user-friendly interface for configuring and running these tests. The tool's efficacy is demonstrated through its application to a native NDK implementation of the AES algorithm.

The Ethereum blockchain has become a widely adopted platform for decentralized applications, attracting a vast array of users. This study examines the transaction ego networks of these users, specifically analyzing how their connected peers are labeled and how these connections evolve over time. We introduce a new methodology for measuring ego network dynamics that incorporates the specific labels of neighboring nodes. Our findings reveal that the structural characteristics of these ego networks vary significantly based on the assigned labels. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the temporal evolution of these networks is non-stationary, indicating that the dynamics of the Ethereum ecosystem are not constant over time.

We report on the observation of Shubnikov-de Haas quantum oscillations in a two-dimensional electron system located at the interface of LaAlO$_3$ and SrTiO$_3$. These oscillations were detected under optical illumination, which was found to be essential for their emergence. The oscillation frequency corresponds to a carrier density of $n_s = 1.1 \times 10^{14}$ cm$^{-2}$, while the effective mass of the carriers is $m^* = 0.15 m_e$.

This paper introduces a novel framework for analyzing the complexity of proof search within logical systems. We demonstrate that this approach successfully characterizes the complexity of proof search in various systems of linear logic, including BV and Pomset logic.
This paper demonstrates the pentagon identity within the Ding-Iohara-Miki algebra by leveraging the quantum dilogarithm's five-term relation.

We present photometric redshifts for 1,000 galaxies within the W-CDF-S and ELAIS-S1 fields, derived from forced photometry spanning 0.36 to 4.5 microns. This dataset was constructed by cross-referencing the WFC3/IRAC and WFC3/UVIS catalogs of the W-CDF-S and ELAIS-S1 fields with the SDSS DR7 catalog. The photometric redshifts were calculated using the Bayesian Estimation of Cosmic Distance (Bayes) method, which incorporates the spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting technique. The resulting photometric redshifts exhibit a median scatter of 0.015 and a mean offset of 0.001.

This study introduces a Bayesian decision support system designed to aid energy systems planners in selecting optimal strategies for the future. The system's core objective is to determine the most advantageous investment portfolio for a specific energy system, accounting for the inherent uncertainties in future conditions. The proposed methodology integrates Bayesian decision theory with a novel, data-driven approach to modeling uncertainty. The framework is demonstrated through a case study involving a hypothetical energy system, where the results are analyzed and discussed.

We demonstrate that the two-electron wavefunction can be represented as a matrix product state with a bond dimension of 3. This representation is derived from the matrix product form of the $N$-electron wavefunction, which possesses a bond dimension of $d$. Specifically, the two-electron wavefunction corresponds to a matrix product state with a bond dimension of $d^2$, where the basis states are formed by the tensor product of two single-electron orbital bases. By utilizing a unitary transformation to diagonalize the single-electron matrix, we reduce this bond dimension from $d^2$ to 3. This reduction relies on the fact that the single-electron matrix is Hermitian and has a rank of at most 3, a consequence of the Pauli exclusion principle. Consequently, the two-electron wavefunction can be expressed as a matrix product state with a bond dimension of 3.

We introduce a non-Abelian dark matter framework featuring a dark sector with a $U(1)_D$ gauge symmetry, where the dark matter particle is a massive vector boson. This model is extended by a $U(1)_L$ lepton-specific gauge symmetry, allowing the dark matter to couple to Standard Model leptons via a $Z_D$ mediator. We demonstrate that this framework can simultaneously account for the observed dark matter relic density and resolve the muon $g-2$ anomaly. Furthermore, we analyze the model's phenomenology, including its experimental signatures and constraints from existing data.

The surge in extreme weather events and rising sea levels has made coastal flooding a critical issue for coastal regions. While high-fidelity models like Delft3D offer detailed simulations, their computational cost is prohibitive for real-time applications. To address this, we introduce a physics-informed neural operator (PINO) surrogate model designed to rapidly predict flood extents and depths. This model utilizes a hybrid loss function combining physics-informed and data-driven components, with the data-driven aspect trained on Delft3D outputs. The study evaluates the model's performance across various scenarios, including those with unseen parameters, and compares it against a purely data-driven neural operator. Results indicate that the PINO achieves superior accuracy and robustness, particularly when handling unseen conditions.

The BeyondPlanck and Cosmoglobe initiatives represent two pivotal, open-access, and reproducible endeavors aimed at analyzing the Planck satellite's full dataset. These projects are designed to foster collaboration, enhance reproducibility, and ensure the long-term accessibility of cosmological data. This paper outlines the specific methodologies employed by these initiatives to achieve these goals, while also addressing the broader challenges inherent in the open science landscape.

This study examines the influence of finite propagation speed on Turing instability within reaction-diffusion systems connected via a network. We demonstrate that a finite propagation speed can induce a Turing instability even when the standard Turing criterion is not met. Furthermore, we show that the spatial arrangement of the network plays a critical role in this phenomenon.

We introduce a quasiclassical framework for Yang-Mills theory, extending the Wigner function formalism to the non-Abelian context. This approach yields a quasiclassical equation of motion for the Wigner function, which serves as a quasiclassical analogue to the Yang-Mills equation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Wigner function can be defined as a phase-space distribution of field-strength tensors.

We present a theoretical investigation into the optical characteristics of wurtzite quantum wires, specifically focusing on polarization anisotropies in spectroscopy. Our findings indicate that the polarization anisotropy of the ground state is governed by the wire's cross-sectional shape. Furthermore, we demonstrate that polarization anisotropies in excited states can be modulated by the wire's aspect ratio. These results are expected to be valuable for interpreting experimental data from spectroscopy of single quantum wires.

Opponent modeling is a critical component of multi-agent systems, yet it remains difficult to apply in real-world scenarios due to the scarcity of data regarding specific opponents. This paper introduces a novel approach to opponent modeling within negotiation dialogues that leverages related data through adaptation. The method employs a two-stage process: first, it constructs a dialogue policy model using available data, and second, it refines this model to fit the characteristics of the target opponent by adapting it from a related data source. The study evaluates this approach across two distinct negotiation environments, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing negotiation performance.

We introduce a novel compactification method for light-like segments, which yields a four-dimensional spacetime paired with a scalar field. This approach is applicable to a wide range of higher-dimensional solutions, including those with non-trivial fluxes, and can be adapted to incorporate Kaluza-Klein reduction. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the resulting four-dimensional theory features a scalar field with a kinetic term that depends dynamically on the scalar field itself.

This study introduces a new online algorithm for constructing balanced designs in sequential experiments. By framing the problem as an online matching task, the method achieves a balance error that is within a factor of two of the optimal minimum. The approach is straightforward to implement and requires no prior knowledge of the total number of experimental units. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that this algorithm is asymptotically optimal for minimizing balance error.

The Si-Al2O3 interface is a critical component in Si-based CMOS technology, serving as the foundation for high-performance devices. This study employs first-principles calculations to investigate the structural and electronic characteristics of this interface, specifically examining how the interface quality correlates with the degree of covalency in the Si-O bond. We demonstrate that the interface quality is governed by the specific termination of the Al2O3 layer, which dictates the resulting Si-O bond character. Furthermore, we identify that the interface's electronic states are primarily determined by the O 2p orbitals, which are modulated by the local coordination environment of the oxygen atoms.

This study introduces a novel approach to estimate the critical mass threshold for black hole formation in spherical gravitational collapse, utilizing non-linear statistical models. We applied this method to the critical collapse solutions of a massless scalar field, a model previously analyzed by Choptuik. Our findings indicate that the critical mass can be estimated with high precision, achieving a relative error of approximately 0.01%.

This study introduces a comprehensive dataset covering the global container shipping sector from 1966 to the present, encompassing freight rates, cargo volumes, newbuilding activity, secondhand and scrap vessel prices, and the count of active ships. The data is sourced from the *Lloyd's List Container Index* and *Lloyd's List Ship Price Index*, with new methods developed to extract and validate information from these publications. The dataset is accessible via the authors' GitHub repository.

This study offers a meta-level analysis of online anomaly detectors, evaluating their performance across various datasets and experimental conditions. We assess the detectors' ability to identify anomalies, their robustness to parameter settings, and their computational efficiency. Our findings indicate that the online Random Cut Forest (RCF) algorithm consistently outperforms other detectors, particularly in scenarios involving a high volume of anomalies.

This study introduces a new approach for segmenting gliomas in brain MRI images by employing a U-Net architecture alongside a novel post-processing method. The proposed method is designed to be computationally efficient, requiring only a single GPU. The model was trained on 1,000 images from the BraTS 2018 dataset, achieving a Dice coefficient of 0.89 for the tumor core and 0.92 for the whole tumor. The post-processing stage utilizes a 3D convolutional neural network to refine the initial segmentation masks, effectively eliminating small noise artifacts and filling gaps in the tumor core.

We present a theoretical framework for creating triplon currents in solids, where triplons represent the elementary magnetic excitations in antiferromagnets. This current generation is driven by a time-varying external magnetic field. The theory is formulated using the framework of linear response, where the triplon current density is expressed as a convolution of the magnetic field's time derivative and a conductivity tensor. This tensor is determined by the imaginary part of the magnetic susceptibility, which is subsequently calculated via the Lehmann representation. The study examines the conductivity tensor's behavior across both low- and high-frequency regimes, alongside its dependence on temperature. Furthermore, we analyze the resulting triplon currents within the context of the Heisenberg model, specifically for both two-dimensional and three-dimensional systems.
This paper introduces the concept of statistical convergence for nets and establishes several relevant theorems.

This study examines the one-dimensional Rosenau equation using the discontinuous Galerkin finite element method. We establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions within the corresponding semi-discrete framework. Furthermore, by employing energy estimates, we derive optimal convergence rates for the fully discrete scheme.

This study examines the well-posedness of a coupled partial differential equation system modeling the interaction between compressible flows and incompressible fluids. The framework integrates the Euler equations for the compressible component with the Navier-Stokes equations for the incompressible one, linked through a shared interface. The analysis relies on a semigroup-based approach, utilizing a specific transformation to decouple the system into two distinct subsystems. The resulting proof establishes the existence of a unique, strongly continuous solution operator within a specific Banach space.

We present a theoretical investigation into the magnetic-field-driven crystallization of charged interlayer excitons in van der Waals heterostructures. Our analysis reveals that the formation of a Wigner crystal is contingent upon the magnetic field surpassing a critical threshold, which is governed by the ratio of the exciton's effective mass to its radius. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the magnetic field can induce a transition from a Wigner crystal to a liquid state, a phenomenon that is highly sensitive to the screening environment.

The Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST) is a Chinese facility designed to deliver a vast number of medium-resolution spectra, making it a critical resource for the study of stellar radial velocities. This paper outlines a relative calibration method for these velocities, which is particularly effective for the LAMOST survey's goal of obtaining radial velocities for approximately 100 million stars. The approach involves correcting for wavelength-dependent distortions in the LAMOST spectrograph using a reference spectrum from a bright, nearby star. This reference spectrum is then subtracted from the target spectrum to align their wavelengths. The study demonstrates that this technique achieves a precision of roughly 0.1 km/s, which is sufficient for the majority of LAMOST's scientific objectives.

This study addresses the inverse scattering problem by determining the spatial distribution of a target's permittivity from its frequency-dependent scattering characteristics. We introduce a novel, fully differentiable forward solver that utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) to compute the scattered field from a given permittivity profile. This approach is designed to handle targets of arbitrary shapes and sizes across a broad spectrum of frequencies. By employing a CNN, we achieve a significant reduction in computational cost compared to traditional Finite-Difference Time-Domain (FDTD) methods. Furthermore, we develop a new inverse solver that leverages the differentiability of our forward model to optimize the permittivity distribution, aiming to minimize the discrepancy between simulated and observed scattering data. This inverse framework is also equipped with a regularization mechanism to ensure the resulting permittivity maps remain physically realistic. We validate the efficacy of our forward and inverse solvers through numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

This study introduces a novel accelerated degradation model based on a bivariate gamma process featuring dependent components. The proposed model incorporates a copula function to capture the dependency structure between two degradation paths, with the specific copula type determined by the correlation coefficient. Furthermore, the paper derives the maximum likelihood estimators for all model parameters and establishes their asymptotic distributions. To evaluate these estimators, a simulation experiment was conducted, followed by an application to real-world data from a lithium-ion battery.

This study examines the triangular flow ($v_3$) in Au+Au and Cu+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$ GeV, utilizing the AMPT model. We analyze the impact of partonic scatterings and hadronic rescatterings on $v_3$ by varying the transport cross sections for quarks and gluons, as well as pions and nucleons. Our results indicate that increasing the transport cross section for quarks and gluons enhances $v_3$ at midrapidity, whereas increasing the cross section for pions and nucleons suppresses it. Furthermore, we observe that the $v_3$ dependence on transverse momentum ($p_T$) is more pronounced in Au+Au collisions than in Cu+Cu collisions.

This study examines the polytropic behavior of plasma within an Interplanetary Coronal Mass Ejection (ICME) interacting with a High-Speed Stream (HSS) by analyzing the 2017 event. Utilizing data from the Advanced Composition Explorer (ACE) and the Wind spacecraft, researchers calculated the polytropic index ($\gamma$) for both the ICME and HSS regions. The findings indicate that the ICME exhibits a polytropic index of $\gamma = 1.1$, whereas the HSS shows a value of $\gamma = 1.3$. These results suggest that the ICME is in a quasi-adiabatic state, while the HSS is in a quasi-isothermal state. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the ICME's plasma undergoes a transition from a quasi-adiabatic to a quasi-isothermal condition as it interacts with the HSS.

The Random Waypoint Mobility Model (RWMM) is a prevalent approach for simulating mobile node behavior in wireless ad hoc networks. This paper introduces a novel RWMM variant that incorporates a minimum separation distance between nodes. We analyze the model's stochastic properties, specifically deriving the probability density functions for node speeds and inter-node distances. Furthermore, we present a simulation framework for this model and validate our theoretical findings through empirical results.

This study examines the effective mass distribution of $K^+K^-$ pairs within the STAR experiment at RHIC, utilizing data from Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$ GeV. The analysis focuses on the region near the kinematic threshold ($2m_K$) and the $\phi$ meson mass. The observed enhancement near the threshold is interpreted as a consequence of the Pauli exclusion principle, whereas the structure around the $\phi$ mass is attributed to the decay of the $\phi$ meson into $K^+K^-$. Additionally, the study evaluates the impact of background contributions from non-resonant $K^+K^-$ pairs and other resonant decays.

This study examines the collective inertial masses of nuclei during reactions, accounting for the influence of the nucleonic effective mass. We demonstrate that the collective inertial mass is not merely the sum of the individual inertial masses of the colliding nuclei. Instead, it is determined by the nucleonic effective mass, which is governed by the nuclear mean field. Consequently, the collective inertial mass is not a constant but varies with the reaction energy.

The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) serves as a benchmark for evaluating an agent's capacity to generalize from examples. While recent studies have demonstrated that deep neural networks can achieve performance on ARC tasks comparable to humans, these models often fail to provide transparent explanations for their decisions. In contrast, this paper introduces a novel search-based approach that generates human-interpretable solutions for ARC tasks. Our method models the task as a constraint satisfaction problem, utilizing a graph representation to define the search space and a graph-guided beam search algorithm to identify solutions. We evaluate this approach on the ARC10K dataset, which comprises 10,000 tasks, and report that it successfully solves 1,000 of them.

This study examines the regularity of entropy solutions to scalar conservation laws featuring a discontinuous flux, specifically $\partial_t u + \partial_x (a(x)f(u)) = 0$, where the coefficient $a(x)$ is a piecewise constant function. We establish that the solution $u$ is continuous within the $W^{s,p}$ space for $s < 1 - 1/p$, provided $s$ and $p$ satisfy the condition $s\gamma + \gamma\beta = 1$, where $\gamma$ and $\beta$ are the magnitudes of the jumps in $a(x)$ at the interface. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the solution exhibits a jump discontinuity in its derivative, with the magnitude of this derivative jump determined by the size of the jump in $a(x)$.

This study determines the branching fractions for the decays $B_{s}^{0} \to D_{s}^{-} K^{+}$ and $B^{0} \to D_{s}^{-} K^{+}$ by analyzing $pp$ collision data at $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV collected by the LHCb experiment. The analysis utilizes a sample of $1.0 \times 10^{9}$ reconstructed $J/\psi \to p\bar{p}$ decays to identify $B_{s}^{0}$ and $B^{0}$ mesons. The branching fractions are derived from the measured decay rates, normalized against the precisely known branching fraction of the $B^{0} \to D^{0} K^{+}$ decay. The resulting values are $\mathcal{B}(B_{s}^{0} \to D_{s}^{-} K^{+}) = (1.00 \pm 0.04 \pm 0.02) \times 10^{-2}$ and $\mathcal{B}(B^{0} \to D_{s}^{-} K^{+}) = (1.00 \pm 0.04 \pm 0.02) \times 10^{-2}$, where the first uncertainty is statistical and the second is systematic.

This study examines the spectral efficiency of cell-free massive MIMO systems employing multicarrier-division duplex (MCD) architectures. We evaluate the performance of both orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) and discrete Fourier transform spread OFDM (DFT-s-OFDM) schemes, analyzing their behavior under varying numbers of subcarriers and pilot sequences. Our findings indicate that, in the limit of an infinite number of subcarriers, the spectral efficiency of OFDM approaches that of single-carrier massive MIMO (SCMIMO) systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the spectral efficiency of DFT-s-OFDM converges toward that of SCMIMMO as the number of pilot sequences increases.

This work examines differential privacy within the shuffle model, a framework where local privacy mechanisms are applied to data before being shuffled by an adversary with limited power. We introduce a new method for deriving lower bounds on privacy loss, which is more precise than existing techniques. Applying this method, we demonstrate that the previously established upper bounds for the shuffle model are optimal for the sum query, a result that extends to a broader class of queries.

This paper introduces a novel modulation scheme named Orthogonal Time Sequency Multiplexing (OTSM). The OTSM signal is generated by applying a time-varying phase modulation to a baseband signal, which is subsequently upconverted to the RF band. The proposed OTSM signal is designed to be orthogonal to both the signal from the preceding symbol and the signal from the subsequent symbol. The paper provides a comprehensive analysis of OTSM, covering its spectral efficiency, spectral occupancy, and power spectral density. Additionally, a low-complexity receiver architecture is proposed, which utilizes a time-domain equalizer to mitigate inter-symbol interference (ISI) and a frequency-domain equalizer to address inter-carrier interference (ICI). The study also examines the bit error rate (BER) performance of OTSM under Rayleigh fading conditions.

This study examines the operator norm within the Banach algebra $\ell^1(S, \omega)$, which is formed by the absolutely summable functions on a discrete semigroup $S$ equipped with a weight $\omega$. We establish that the norm of any element in this algebra is determined by its action on the Banach space $C_b(S, \omega)$, consisting of bounded functions on $S$ under the weight $\omega$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the algebra is unital if and only if the weight $\omega$ is finitely supported.

This study numerically investigates the dynamics of a molten metal melt pool during laser spot melting, focusing on the influence of laser power, beam radius, and scanning speed. The analysis employs a two-dimensional axisymmetric model that accounts for laser energy absorption, surface tension, and Marangoni convection. The results indicate that the melt pool's shape and dimensions are governed by the laser power, beam radius, and scanning speed. Specifically, the melt pool's depth and width increase with higher laser power and beam radius, whereas the scanning speed has a negligible effect on these dimensions.

This study investigates a wireless energy transfer and mobile edge computing framework designed for public transport vehicles, where a mobile edge computing server (MEC-S) is mounted on a bus to facilitate data offloading and energy replenishment for connected devices. To enhance communication efficiency, an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) is integrated into the bus's interior. The primary objective is to maximize the total computing capacity of the MEC-S by jointly optimizing the transmit power of the base station, the phase shifts of the IRS, and the bus's trajectory. This optimization is achieved through a two-stage approach: first, the bus's path is optimized using a convex optimization technique, followed by the application of a block coordinate descent algorithm to refine the transmit power and IRS phase shifts. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed scheme significantly outperforms existing benchmark methods.

We establish a lower bound on the approximate degree of a function defined by a DNF formula, expressed in terms of its sensitivity and the count of variables appearing in the formula at most once. This result extends a finding by Sherstov regarding the approximate degree of a DNF formula with bounded degree to match a lower bound defined by its block sensitivity. Additionally, we derive a matching upper bound for the approximate degree of a CNF formula, determined by its block sensitivity and the count of variables appearing in the formula at most once.

This study introduces a novel method for detecting bistable structures in dynamical systems by utilizing the Conley index. We demonstrate that the Conley index can be approximated through the persistent homology of a discrete-time dynamical system. Furthermore, we apply this approach to identify bistable structures in biological models, specifically the FitzHugh-Nagumo equation and the Schnakenberg reaction-diffusion system.

This study examines the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars under finite temperature and magnetic field conditions. We employ the MIT bag model to describe the equation of state for the quark matter within the star, while utilizing the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations to determine the stellar structure. Our analysis reveals that the presence of a magnetic field and non-zero temperature significantly influence the star's structural properties.

Audio-visual correlation (AVC) involves learning the relationship between audio and video data, a field that has seen significant advancements in recent years. This paper reviews recent progress in AVC, covering both traditional and deep learning-based methods. We also examine the primary hurdles in current research and outline potential future research directions.

The Linear Ordering Problem (LOP) is a combinatorial optimization challenge with applications in diverse fields, including sports scheduling, network design, and social choice theory. This study introduces a novel probabilistic framework for assessing the reliability of LOP solutions. We propose a new method to calculate the probability of a specific solution being optimal, along with a corresponding algorithm that leverages this probability to identify the most reliable outcomes. Additionally, we present a heuristic approach designed to locate the solution with the highest reliability. Computational experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods.

This study investigates the impact of granularity on the superconducting properties of NbN films, specifically examining how the transition from the superconducting to normal state is influenced by granularity. We report that the superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$) in these films is highly sensitive to the measurement frequency, a phenomenon attributed to the presence of superconducting islands within a non-superconducting matrix. Furthermore, we observe that the critical current ($I_c$) exhibits a marked dependence on both temperature and frequency, a behavior explained by the interplay between thermal fluctuations and phase fluctuations.

Temporal graphs are gaining significant traction in domains like social networks, transportation systems, and biological research. A temporal graph consists of a graph structure where edges are assigned timestamps, representing the specific time they exist. A temporal walk is defined as a sequence of edges where each edge's timestamp is no earlier than that of the preceding one. This paper introduces a novel query language designed to retrieve temporal walks within such graphs. We demonstrate that evaluating this language is NP-hard, yet we also present a set of tractable conditions. Furthermore, we developed a practical algorithm that leverages these conditions to efficiently evaluate queries.

This study introduces a novel method for decelerating polyatomic free radicals using a simultaneous Zeeman deceleration technique involving the free radical and lithium atoms. The approach leverages the magnetic moment of lithium atoms to enhance the deceleration efficiency of the radicals. Theoretical analysis indicates that this method can reduce the velocity of the methylidyne radical (CH) to 100 m/s, a significant improvement over the 200 m/s limit achievable with conventional Zeeman deceleration.

The Swift-XRT Living Swift-XRT Point Source catalogue (LSXPS) is a continuously updated collection of X-ray sources identified by the X-Ray Telescope aboard the Swift satellite. This catalogue is maintained in real-time by the Real-Time Transient Detector (RTTD), which identifies significant events by analyzing the light curves of all observed sources. The RTTD operates by comparing the current flux of a source against its historical average, flagging any source with a flux exceeding 100 times the mean as a transient. This paper outlines the RTTD's operational principles and its role in generating the LSXPS. Furthermore, we demonstrate the detector's efficacy by presenting a selection of notable transient events detected by the RTTD.

We investigate the plaquette valence bond state (PVB S) within the spin-1/2 J1-J2 XY model on a square lattice, where the J1 and J2 terms represent competing nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor XY interactions, respectively. By employing the variational Monte Carlo method, we analyze the ground state phase diagram and identify a distinct PVB S phase situated between the Néel and plaquette phases. Furthermore, we examine the characteristics of this PVB S phase, including its excitation spectrum and correlation functions.

This study introduces a three-dimensional panel data model designed to analyze bilateral trade flows, accounting for the influence of both exporter and importer characteristics. The model decomposes these flows into three distinct components: a common factor reflecting shared traits of trading partners, exporter-specific factors, and importer-specific factors. The common factor is derived from a factor model, while the remaining two components are estimated using a panel regression framework. The authors demonstrate that consistent estimates for the parameters of both the factor model and the panel regression can be achieved even when the number of factors is unknown, provided the number of trading partners is sufficiently large. The paper further establishes the asymptotic normality of these parameter estimates. Finally, the proposed model is applied to decompose global trade flows, with the results indicating that common factor effects account for a substantial portion of trade volume.

This study examines the construction of four-dimensional noncommutative deformations of $U(1)$ gauge theory, specifically those compatible with a constant background field. We demonstrate that these theories can be formulated as a consistent $L_{\infty}$ algebra, with the $L_{\infty}$ structure constants defined by the background field. Furthermore, we establish a method to derive these $L_{\infty}$ structures by bootstrapping them from the $L_{\infty}$ algebra of Moyal plane field theory.

This study introduces a coherent equalization framework for linear quantum systems, designed to counteract detrimental effects like attenuation and phase distortion. By leveraging coherent feedback, the proposed method offers a streamlined and computationally efficient approach to quantum equalization. We demonstrate that the equalization problem can be resolved by solving a specific Riccati equation, with the resulting solution derived via a coherent quantum Kalman filter. Furthermore, the paper establishes the necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of a quantum Kalman filter.

Perceiving the passage of time is a fundamental human capability that is significantly altered in individuals with mental disorders. This study introduces a novel approach to continuously and automatically monitor time perception in people with depression using wearable sensors. The method involves presenting participants with a series of unpredictable visual stimuli while they wear a smartwatch, which records their heart rate variability (HRV). The system then estimates the perceived duration of each stimulus by calculating the ratio between the HRV during the stimulus and the HRV during the inter-stimulus interval. The accuracy of this estimation is evaluated by comparing the predicted durations against the actual stimulus lengths. The results demonstrate that this approach effectively and continuously tracks time perception in real-world settings.

This study investigates the trade-off between decision quality and speed in a natural setting, utilizing data from a high-stakes, complex decision-making task involving the identification of concealed objects within images. We observe that individuals tend to prioritize accuracy over speed when the consequences of errors are severe, yet this preference shifts when the likelihood of making mistakes is low. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the optimal balance between speed and quality is contingent upon the specific task at hand.

This paper examines the legal compatibility of various fairness definitions by analyzing how they align with the disparate impact standard. We demonstrate that while the four most prevalent definitions—demographic parity, equalized odds, equal opportunity, and fairness through unawareness—can be framed as specific instances of disparate impact, they are not universally so. Furthermore, we identify that these definitions are not interchangeable; they can yield conflicting outcomes. Consequently, we argue that the disparate impact standard remains the most robust and legally sound approach for evaluating fairness.

This magnetization arises from the interaction between the neutrino pair's spin and the ion's electron spin. The proposed system is capable of detecting both electron and antineutrinos, as well as electron and antineutrinos, with a detection efficiency of 100%.
